AUSTIN, Texas, Nov. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Oracle (NYSE: ORCL) will hold its 2026 Annual Meeting of Stockholders on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, at 9:00 a.m., Central Time. This year's meeting will be conducted virtually via a live audio webcast at www.virtualshareholdermeeting.com/ORCL2026. Stockholders as of the close of business on September 21, 2026, the record date, are entitled to participate in the Annual Meeting. Guests may also view the Annual Meeting but may not vote or ask questions.

The proxy materials and website www.virtualshareholdermeeting.com/ORCL2026 include instructions on how to participate in the meeting and how stockholders may vote their shares of Oracle stock. A recording of the meeting will be available at www.virtualshareholdermeeting.com/ORCL2026 and on our Investor Relations website at www.oracle.com/investor following the Annual Meeting through November 25, 2026.

About Oracle
Oracle offers integrated suites of applications plus secure, autonomous infrastructure in the Oracle Cloud. For more information about Oracle (NYSE: ORCL), please visit us at www.oracle.com.

title: Ezra Klein Floats “the End of Oracle” as OpenAI Weighs Smaller Data Center Plans
detail:
Ezra Klein Floats “the End of Oracle” as OpenAI Weighs Smaller Data Center Plans
Roxanna Maglangit

ORCL

Trade Oracle on Coinbase

Ezra Klein Floats "the End of Oracle" as OpenAI Weighs Smaller Data Center Plans ©v2killer7603 from pixabay and spxChrome from Getty Images Signature DanielPrudek from Getty Images and Burak The Weekender from Pexels Bianca Constantinescu's Images and Madalina Vasilica's Imags from Canva
Key Takeaways

After this week's elections, OpenAI's senior leaders discussed whether to reset next year's data center capacity plans, the Wall Street Journal reported, and Ezra Klein raised "the end of Oracle" on the Hard Fork podcast.

Klein's line is hyperbole, but Oracle is the big company most exposed to a smaller OpenAI build, since S&P says OpenAI accounts for about half of its $664 billion backlog.

Oracle spent $55.7 billion on capex in fiscal 2026, its total debt reached $167 billion, and analysts expect negative free cash flow through fiscal 2028.

An anonymous seller is auctioning about $500 million of data center loans, including one tied to Oracle's Stargate site in New Mexico, with bids due Nov. 19.

The midterm fallout just reached the biggest customer of Oracle (ORCL:NYSE).

By Wednesday morning, senior leaders at OpenAI were discussing whether Tuesday's results meant the company would have to reset its expectations for data center capacity next year. The Wall Street Journal reported that, citing a person familiar with the conversation.

Goldman Sachs has warned that Democratic wins at the state and local level could put 45% of planned US data center capacity at risk.

Then New York Times columnist Ezra Klein went on the paper's Hard Fork podcast. He was laying out a contrarian take he'd seen going around: that a slower, politically paced build-out might actually be good for investors. Along the way, he raised "the end of Oracle" as one possible result.

Hyperbole? Probably. But Oracle has made it a fair question.

OpenAI's build is mostly Oracle's

S&P has said OpenAI accounts for about half of Oracle's backlog, which stood at $664 billion of contracted revenue on Aug. 31.

And OpenAI leans on Oracle just as hard. Reacting to the Journal's report on X, AI critic Ed Zitron wrote that "openai's capex is mostly A) Oracle's clunky, over-expensive and ever-delayed buildout."

So when OpenAI talks about resetting its capacity plans, it's mostly talking about Oracle's.

Oracle has already spent the money

Oracle's free cash flow went from $11.8 billion in fiscal 2024 (its years end in May) to negative $23.7 billion in fiscal 2026. Analysts expect it to stay negative for two more years:

Oracle (ORCL): free cash flow, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2024-2029 (years to May) (TIKR)

Analysts see free cash flow turning positive at $17.5 billion in fiscal 2029. That's well below the more than $30 billion Oracle targeted for that year at its Oct. 28 Investor Day, and both figures assume OpenAI keeps taking capacity on schedule.

title: How AI spending limits could help hyperscaler bonds but hurt stocks
detail:
How AI spending limits could help hyperscaler bonds but hurt stocks
Investing.com
Fri, November 6, 2026 at 1:24 PM MST 3 min read
ORCL
SPCX
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Investing.com -- A regulatory brake on AI data-center spending could be good for hyperscaler bonds and bad for their stocks. The two groups want different things from the same company.

Still guessing which stocks will beat the market? Our AI portfolio updates monthly and is outperforming the S&P 500 by 118%. See this month's list »

Why bondholders could win

Less borrowing. Slower data-center building means fewer new bond issues. That leaves less debt against the same earnings.

More cash left over. If the capacity is "already sold," revenue from existing contracts keeps arriving. With less capital spending, more of it is free cash flow, which is what covers interest and principal.

A fixed payoff. A bondholder who holds to maturity gets the coupon plus principal and nothing extra. Safety matters more than growth.

Why shareholders lose

Equity values future growth. Slower expansion could cap future income, so stocks absorb the damage. The same applies to the China risk. If US firms are slowed and Chinese rivals gain ground, shareholders lose the upside. Bondholders mostly don't, unless the loss gets bad enough to threaten repayment.

Unsure what to buy ahead of earnings? Our AI's recent pre-earnings calls delivered gains of +77% to +118% after results dropped. See this month's earnings picks »

The author flags one real danger for bonds: a company that grows faster than it can afford. That is a credit problem, and it is where the brake could help.

What spreads are saying

A spread is the extra yield a bond pays over a safe benchmark, so it measures perceived credit risk. Wider spreads mean the market demands more compensation.

Hyperscaler spreads have widened in recent weeks. Most of it comes from Oracle and SpaceX, which the market already treats as risky because they keep burning cash.

It isn't only hyperscalers. Sector spreads still rose after the six hyperscalers were removed. That points to a broader pullback in credit risk appetite, which began before the US midterm election. AI-spending worries are part of the cause.

High-grade credit is calm. The Bloomberg US Corporate index spread rose 2 bps Thursday after falling 2 bps Wednesday. Despite this week's volatility, investment-grade credit barely moved.

High yield is volatile but flat on the week. Spreads closed Thursday where they were last Friday. The author notes hyperscalers aren't in junk "yet", which hints that a deterioration could eventually push them there.

Takeaways

A spending cap shifts value from future growth, which stocks price, to current cash flow, which bonds price.

Much of the recent widening comes from a few cash-burning names, not the whole group.

The broad credit market hasn't panicked. The unease is concentrated and still building.

Bloom Energy Rises 2%, AMD Up 8% as AI Stocks Rebound From Midterm Rout ©@pisitkhambubpha via Canva, @vanitjan via Canva
Key Takeaways

Bloom Energy rose 2% today as AI stocks, AMD among them, bounced back from Thursday's post-midterm selloff.

Bloom had just landed a 900-megawatt NTT DATA deal and a 1-gigawatt plan with California Resources.

Analysts expect Bloom's normalized EPS to climb from $0.76 in 2025 to $8.24 in 2028. Slower US data-center building is the main risk.

Oracle's Dec. 10 report and GE Vernova's turbine orders are the next reads on that demand.

Bloom Energy (BE:NYSE) is up 2% today as AI and data-center stocks bounce back from Thursday's rout after Democrats won control of Congress. Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ) is up 8%.

Bloom fell 16% on Thursday after a week of new demand. It got a 900-megawatt deal with NTT DATA and a plan with California Resources (CRC) for 1 gigawatt or more of fuel cells, on top of its 2.8-gigawatt Oracle (ORCL:NYSE) deal. GE Vernova (GEV:NYSE), which sells turbines into the same buildout, reported third-quarter orders up 96% organically.

The fear is about 2028

UBS analysts estimate construction pauses could put about 30% of the US data-center capacity expected in 2028 at risk. Bloom made 97% of its third-quarter revenue in the US.

AMD fell 17% on Thursday even though its third-quarter revenue rose 45% to $13.4 billion, with data-center sales up 97%, and CEO Lisa Su expects growth "to accelerate further in the fourth quarter."

Bloom's earnings are still headed up

Analysts expect Bloom's normalized EPS to grow more than tenfold from 2025 to 2028:

Bloom Energy (BE): normalized EPS, actual and consensus estimates, $ per share, fiscal 2023-2028 (TIKR)

Yet at Thursday's close Bloom traded at about 40x forward earnings, against a one-year average of 112x.

TIKR tracks 29 analysts on Bloom Energy. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Bloom Energy, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Bloom Energy's Analyst Ratings

Oracle is the one to watch

Oracle's free cash flow was negative $5 billion in its quarter ended Aug. 31 as it builds data centers. Its Dec. 10 report will show whether it's sticking with that spending, and the 2.8 gigawatts Bloom is counting on.

GE Vernova's backlog hit $197 billion, and CEO Scott Strazik said on its third-quarter call that it's taking gas turbine reservations for delivery in 2032. Every year a data center waits for a turbine is another year Bloom can pitch power in about 90 days.

California Resources' plan is a non-binding memorandum of understanding that still needs contracts, a final investment decision and EPA permits. Its 2027 budget, out with its fourth-quarter results, will show whether it's funding the project.

Oracle Corp. Meta and Alphabet climbed 0.4% apiece as Amazon slipped 1% and Microsoft slid 1.5%.The value discrepancy reflects how investors are valuing key cloud and technology businesses despite uncertainties about investing on AI infrastructure.But a better relative valuation rating doesn't always suggest Oracle has less risk.The corporation still has big data-center investment needs and doubts about how much return such projects will deliver.The next trigger will be if the IT sector bounce continues and investors re-rate Oracle on its capital investment and earnings projections.
